questions.enonce_markdown:
A standard solution of a 0.18 mol dm$^{-3}$ sulphuric acid was prepared, 21.6 cm$^3$ of the solution neutralized 25.0 cm$^3$ of a sodium hydroxide solution. On evaporation and weighing, 0.30 g of the salt $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ was obtained.

(i) What is a standard solution?

(ii) Calculate the molarity of sodium hydroxide solution

(iii) Determine the mass of $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ expected.

(iv) Calculate the percentage yield of the reaction *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Standard solution.** A standard solution is a solution whose **concentration is accurately known** (for example, prepared by dissolving an accurately weighed mass of a pure, stable solute in a known volume of solution in a volumetric flask).

**(ii) Molarity of NaOH.** Equation: $\mathrm{H_2SO_4} + 2\mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_2SO_4} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$

$n(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}) = 0.18 \times \dfrac{21.6}{1000} = 3.888\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$

Mole ratio $\mathrm{H_2SO_4} : \mathrm{NaOH} = 1 : 2$, so $n(\mathrm{NaOH}) = 2 \times 3.888\times10^{-3} = 7.776\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ in 25.0 cm$^3$.

$$[\mathrm{NaOH}] = \frac{7.776\times10^{-3}}{25.0/1000} = \mathbf{0.311\ mol\ dm^{-3}}$$

**(iii) Mass of $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$ expected.** Mole ratio $\mathrm{H_2SO_4} : \mathrm{Na_2SO_4} = 1 : 1$, so $n(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}) = 3.888\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$.

$M(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}) = 2(23) + 32.0 + 4(16.0) = 142\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}$

$$m = 3.888\times10^{-3} \times 142 = \mathbf{0.552\ g}$$

**(iv) Percentage yield.**

$$\text{percentage yield} = \frac{\text{actual mass}}{\text{expected mass}} \times 100 = \frac{0.30}{0.552} \times 100 = \mathbf{54.3\ \%}$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
The reaction $2\mathrm{NO(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO_2(g)}$ is in equilibrium at 503 K. The concentrations of the species at equilibrium in mol dm$^{-3}$ are: $[\mathrm{NO}] = 0.03$, $[\mathrm{NO_2}] = 8.9$, $[\mathrm{O_2}] = 0.07$

(i) State the equilibrium law

(ii) Write the expression for the equilibrium constant

(iii) Calculate the value for the equilibrium constant ($K_c$) stating its units. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Equilibrium law.** At a **given temperature**, when a reversible reaction has reached dynamic equilibrium, the **product of the equilibrium concentrations of the products, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation, divided by the product of the equilibrium concentrations of the reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient, is a constant** (the equilibrium constant, $K_c$).

**(ii) Expression.**

$$K_c = \frac{[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2}{[\mathrm{NO}]^2\,[\mathrm{O_2}]}$$

**(iii) Value and units.**

$$K_c = \frac{(8.9)^2}{(0.03)^2 \times 0.07} = \frac{79.21}{6.3\times10^{-5}} = 1.26\times10^{6}$$

Units: $\dfrac{(\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})^2}{(\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})^2(\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})} = \mathrm{mol^{-1}\,dm^{3}}$.

$$\boxed{K_c = 1.26\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}}}\ \text{(at 503 K)}$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the following standard electrode potentials for the following half cells:

$\mathrm{Pb^{2+}} + 2e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Pb(s)}$   $E^\circ = -0.13\ \mathrm{V}$

$\mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn(s)}$   $E^\circ = -0.76\ \mathrm{V}$

(i) Write the overall equation for the cell reaction.

(ii) Draw the cell diagram for the combination of the two half cells. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The half-cell with the **more negative** $E^\circ$ (zinc, $-0.76$ V) is the **negative electrode** (anode), where oxidation occurs; the lead half-cell ($-0.13$ V) is the **positive electrode** (cathode), where reduction occurs.

**(i) Overall cell reaction:**

$$\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Pb^{2+}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Pb(s)}$$

$E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{\text{positive}} - E^\circ_{\text{negative}} = (-0.13) - (-0.76) = +0.63\ \mathrm{V}$ (positive, so the reaction is feasible).

**(ii) Cell diagram** (anode on the left, cathode on the right, double bar for the salt bridge):

$$\mathrm{Zn(s)\ |\ Zn^{2+}(aq)\ \|\ Pb^{2+}(aq)\ |\ Pb(s)} \qquad E^\circ_{cell} = +0.63\ \mathrm{V}$$

Electrons flow in the external circuit from the zinc electrode to the lead electrode.

questions.enonce_markdown: Calculate the pH of a 0.25 M solution of calcium hydroxide, $\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}$ *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Calcium hydroxide is a strong base (taken as fully dissociated) and each formula unit gives **two** hydroxide ions:

$$\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}$$

$[\mathrm{OH^-}] = 2 \times 0.25 = 0.50\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}$

$\mathrm{pOH} = -\log_{10}(0.50) = 0.30$

At 25 $^\circ$C, $\mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH} = 14$ (that is, $K_w = 1.0\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{mol^2\,dm^{-6}}$):

$$\mathrm{pH} = 14 - 0.30 = \mathbf{13.70}$$

(Same result from $[\mathrm{H^+}] = K_w/[\mathrm{OH^-}] = 2.0\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$, $\mathrm{pH} = 13.70$.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Ethanol (boiling point 78 $^\circ$C) and propanone (boiling point 56 $^\circ$C) form a completely miscible solution that deviates positively from Raoult's law.

(i) State Raoult's law

(ii) Why does the mixture deviate positively from Raoult's law?

(iii) Draw a well labeled graph of vapour pressure against composition for the mixture *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Raoult's law.** For an ideal solution, the **partial vapour pressure of a component at a given temperature is equal to the mole fraction of that component in the liquid multiplied by the vapour pressure of the pure component at that temperature**: $p_A = x_A\,p_A^{\circ}$. (The total vapour pressure is $P = p_A + p_B$.)

**(ii) Reason for the positive deviation.** In pure ethanol the molecules are held together by **hydrogen bonds**. When propanone is added, the propanone molecules (which cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other) **break some of the ethanol hydrogen bonds**, and the new ethanol-propanone attractions (permanent dipole - hydrogen bond-type interactions) are **weaker than the average of the ethanol-ethanol and propanone-propanone attractions** in the pure liquids. The molecules therefore escape from the mixture more easily than in an ideal solution, so the **vapour pressure is higher than Raoult's law predicts**. Energy is absorbed on mixing (the enthalpy of mixing is positive, $\Delta H_{mix} > 0$; the mixture cools) and the volume increases slightly.

**(iii) Graph.** To draw:

- **x-axis:** composition, from pure propanone on the left (mole fraction of ethanol $= 0$) to pure ethanol on the right (mole fraction of ethanol $= 1$); **y-axis:** vapour pressure (at constant temperature).
- Mark the vapour pressures of the pure liquids on the two vertical axes: $p^\circ_{\text{propanone}}$ (higher, the more volatile, b.p. 56 $^\circ$C) on the left and $p^\circ_{\text{ethanol}}$ (lower) on the right.
- Draw as a **dashed straight line** joining these two values the **ideal** total vapour pressure (Raoult's law).
- Draw the **real total vapour pressure** as a **curve that lies above the ideal straight line** between the two end points, rising to a **maximum** at an intermediate composition (higher than the vapour pressure of either pure liquid). Label it "positive deviation". The partial-pressure curves of each component also lie above their dashed ideal straight lines.
- The maximum in vapour pressure corresponds to a **minimum in boiling point** (a minimum-boiling azeotrope, which cannot be separated completely by fractional distillation).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The relative abundance of each naturally-occurring lead isotope is given as follows:

| Isotope | % abundance |
|---|---|
| $^{204}\mathrm{Pb}$ | 2 |
| $^{206}\mathrm{Pb}$ | 25 |
| $^{207}\mathrm{Pb}$ | 21 |
| $^{208}\mathrm{Pb}$ | 52 |

(i) What are isotopes?

(ii) Calculate the relative abundance of lead. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Isotopes** are **atoms of the same element (same atomic number, same number of protons) that have different numbers of neutrons**, and therefore different mass numbers. They have the same chemical properties (same electronic configuration) but slightly different physical properties.

**(ii)** The quantity that is calculated from the isotopic abundances is the **relative atomic mass** of lead (the question's "relative abundance of lead" is read as this). It is the weighted mean of the isotopic masses:

$$A_r(\mathrm{Pb}) = \frac{(204\times2) + (206\times25) + (207\times21) + (208\times52)}{100} = \frac{408 + 5150 + 4347 + 10816}{100} = \frac{20721}{100}$$

$$\boxed{A_r(\mathrm{Pb}) = 207.21 \approx 207.2}$$

(The abundances add up to $2 + 25 + 21 + 52 = 100\ \%$.)
